# Answer key - Chapter 01: Cloud computing and information security {.unnumbered}

<!-- Source-only: this directory is excluded from the render in _quarto.yml
     ("!answers/"). Never link these files from a chapter. Numbering must
     match the chapter's Self-check section 1:1. -->

**Q1** *(tests @sec-01-definition-cloud-computing · basic)* - **Correct: c.**
The chapter states that of the five characteristics, resource pooling produces
most of the security questions in this course, because sharing hardware with
strangers is exactly what a traditional data centre never did
(@sec-01-definition-cloud-computing).

**Q2** *(tests @sec-01-cia-triad · basic)* - **Correct: d.**
Per @def-cia and @exm-nextcloud-cia, an attacker who merely makes the service
unreachable when it is needed attacks availability without reading or altering
anything; the distractors confuse the three properties or assume all attacks
must touch data.

**Q3** *(tests @sec-01-threat-risk-control · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
"Risk is the weight of a threat, expressed as likelihood times impact",
"likelihood × impact", "risk = likelihood times impact of a threat"
(any phrasing that names likelihood and impact and ties risk to a threat,
per @def-trc).

**Q4** *(tests @sec-01-service-models · basic)* - **Correct: b.**
The data row never leaves the customer's column in @tbl-sharedresp: even in
SaaS the customer decides who may access which data and what published data
reveals. Virtualisation, networking and (in PaaS/SaaS) the operating system
move to the provider.

**Q5** *(tests @sec-01-why-cloud-security · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
any two of: "lack of control and visibility", "infrastructure shared with
outsiders", "large number of services with dependencies (larger attack
surface)", "constantly changing set of running instances", "remote access for
all users", "heavy use of software from the provider and third parties"
(Comer's six factors, @sec-01-why-cloud-security).

**Q6** *(tests @sec-01-why-cloud-security · basic)* - **Correct: c.**
The chapter stresses that no system was breached and no password stolen: the
failure was a governance decision - somebody chose what to publish without
reasoning about what could be inferred from it (@exm-strava).

**Q7 - applied scenario** *(tests @sec-01-service-models · applied)* -
**Model answer:** Tasks that move to the provider (any two): operating-system
patching, web-server/TLS configuration, server hardening, firewall management,
hardware and hypervisor security. Responsibility that stays: the data row -
deciding who may access which data and what shared/published data reveals
(identities and configuration also acceptable). Why the claim is wrong: per
@tbl-sharedresp the data row never leaves the customer's column, and the
Strava case (@exm-strava) shows exactly this kind of customer-side governance
decision failing even though no system was breached; the chapter concludes
that no service model exists in which security is entirely somebody else's
problem. **Grading notes:** full credit needs (a) two provider-side tasks,
(b) the data/governance responsibility that stays, and (c) an explicit link
to Strava or the "data row stays with the customer" rule. Partial credit for
correctly split responsibilities without the Strava argument.

## Sketch answers to the chapter exercises

(1) *(@exr-01-five-characteristics - Five essential characteristics)*
Self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity,
measured service: portal instead of ticket; created from anywhere; capacity
was standing by, shared; one machine can become ten; billed by the hour.

(2) *(@exr-01-strava-cia - Strava case, in CIA terms)*
Confidentiality of the bases, not of the individuals; aggregation
re-identified what anonymisation hid, so the governance decision to publish was
the failure.

(3) *(@exr-01-trc-vulnerability - Threat, risk, control for a vulnerability)*
The customer's: in IaaS the customer manages from the operating
system upward (@def-servicemodels, @tbl-sharedresp).

(4) *(@exr-01-open-ssh-port - Open SSH port as threat–risk–control)*
Threat: an attacker brute-forces SSH credentials. Risk: high likelihood
(constant automated scanning) times high impact (full control). Control:
key-only login restricted to the administrative address.

(5) *(@exr-01-saas-reduces-risk - When SaaS reduces the risk)*
SaaS removes OS patching, TLS configuration and server hardening; it does not
remove deciding who may access which data, because the data row stays with the
customer.
